title: Noise Tolerance of Distributionally Robust Learning
claim: A standard distributionally robust baseline degrades faster than plain least-squares as noise grows, so robustness is not guaranteed.
layout: 1 panel, line plot, two series, legend top-left
description: A single matplotlib line chart on a grid background. The x-axis is noise level, running from 0 to 3. The y-axis is relative error in percent, running from 0 to about 190. Two series are drawn with diamond markers. The red line is WDRL Regression. The green line is MSE Regression. Both start near 5–8% error at noise 0. The red line then climbs to about 50% at noise 1, about 89% at noise 2 and about 190% at noise 3. The green line stays lower, at about 17%, 34% and 146% at those same noise levels. The gap between the lines widens as noise increases. A legend in the upper left names the two methods. The eye goes first to the steep red curve. The proposed Wasserstein-loss method does not appear in the plot.
caption: Test error evolution for Navier-Stokes operator learning with 30% corrupted training data with Cauchy noise
abstract: Given the importance of building robust machine learning models, considerable efforts have recently been put into developing training strategies that achieve robustness to outliers and adversarial attacks. Yet, a major aspect that remains an open problem is systematic robustness to global forms of noise such as those that come from measurements and quantization. Hence, we propose in this work an approach to train regression models from data with additive forms of noise, leveraging the Wasserstein distance as a loss function. Importantly, our approach is agnostic to the model structure, unlike the increasingly popular Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Learning paradigm (WDRL) which, we show, does not achieve improved robustness when the regression function is not convex or Lipschitz. We provide a theoretical analysis of the scaling of the regression functions in terms of the variance of the noise, for both formulations and show consistency of the proposed loss function. Lastly, we conclude with numerical experiments on physical PDE Benchmarks and electric grid data, demonstrating competitive performance with an order of magnitude reduction in computational cost.
